units.claim: Three separate credentials exist and are unequal: an organizer account session, an entrant token, and a room (seat) token.
units.notes: All three exist and are checked at runtime: account_for_session() resolves the session cookie, entrant_from_token() resolves ?token=, get_player(code, x_player_token) resolves the seat header. An additional fourth credential (admin) exists but is out of this contract's base path — see divergences.

units.claim: The organizer session is carried in a `session` cookie that is httpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
units.notes: Attributes are all correct (httponly=True, secure=True, samesite="lax", path="/", max_age=SESSION_DAYS*86400), but the cookie's name is `table_session`, not `session`. Anyone implementing a client from §1 would read the wrong cookie name.

units.claim: require_organizer matches the session's account against tournaments.organizer_account_id and is the authorization chokepoint for organizer actions.
units.notes: Every mutating tournament endpoint (entrants, release/drop/undrop, end, rounds, close, result, time, timer, call ack/resolve) routes through require_organizer; grep of app/tournaments.py shows no organizer-mutating route bypassing it.

units.claim: Any account other than the owner gets 403.
units.notes: HTTPException(403, "only the organizer can do that"). Code additionally emits a security_event(AUTHZ_DENY, username, path) audit record, which §1 does not mention (see divergences, low).

units.claim: No session gets 401.
units.notes: require_account raises 401 "sign in first" and is called before the ownership lookup, so an unauthenticated caller gets 401 even for a nonexistent tournament code.

units.claim: POST /claim takes no authentication at all; possession of the tournament code is the gate and it returns a tournament-scoped token.
units.notes: claim(code, body) takes no Request and no cookie/token parameter — it cannot read a session even accidentally. Token is secrets.token_urlsafe(24) stored on entrants.token, which is scoped by tournament_code in entrant_from_token (tournaments.py:166-169).

units.claim: entrants.account_id is never written; it exists only as a hook for a future opt-in history link.
units.notes: The column exists in the entrants schema; a repo-wide grep for account_id in backend/app finds no INSERT or UPDATE targeting entrants.account_id — the only writes are to players.account_id / sessions / tournaments.organizer_account_id. Correctly a defined-but-unwritten column, as documented.

units.claim: The anonymity guarantee is pinned by TestIdentityStaysSeparate.
units.notes: Class exists with three tests: claim needs no account, a signed-in claim leaves entrants.account_id NULL, and the roster body contains no "account". Tests could not be executed — backend/.venv does not exist in this checkout — so this is a static verification of their presence and assertions.

units.claim: Entrant tokens are query parameters, not headers.
units.notes: Every entrant-authenticated route takes `token: str | None = None` as a query parameter; no backend route reads an entrant token from a header. Note the spec's rationale ("reads from a plain GET") is only partly true — POST /pods/{id}/call and POST /pods/{id}/turn also carry the token in the URL.

units.claim: Because the entrant token rides in the URL it must never be logged: the reverse proxy strips query strings from access logs.
units.notes: No query-string stripping exists anywhere. The site block is `encode gzip` + `header -Server` + `reverse_proxy mtg:8000` with no `log` directive and no URI/query rewriting; the root Caddyfile's only global block is `servers { trusted_proxies … }`. Worse, the app is started as plain `uvicorn app.main:app`, whose access log is on by default and writes the full request line including `?token=…` to container logs. The app has no logging middleware that would redact it. This is the section's one substantive safety claim and it is unbacked.

units.claim: GET /{code} returns a room token only on myPod.roomToken, for the caller's own seat, derived from their entrant token, and it never appears in pods[].
units.notes: pod_views entries contain podId/table/status/roomCode(organizer-only)/extensionSeconds/turnsRemaining/seats, and seats carry only seat, entrantId, name, place, points — no room_token. my_pod is built only when the viewer's entrant id matches a seat (`mine`), and only then adds roomToken and roomCode. Anonymous callers get viewer_entrant=None, hence no myPod.

units.claim: Three tests in test_tournaments.py::TestPlayerView pin the room-token rule.
units.notes: Exactly three of the class's tests are about the room token (own token opens the room; token never leaks into pods[]/seats; anonymous viewer gets none). Not executed — no backend/.venv present.

units.claim: The room token is carried in the X-Player-Token header on the table API and grants one seat in one room.
units.notes: Tournament pods mint one players row per seat with its own token and store it on pod_seats.room_token; the table API resolves it per-room via get_player(code, x_player_token), so a token is scoped to a single room and seat.

units.claim: There is no clock stored in a room and nothing syncing one; every client counts down locally against one absolute server deadline.
units.notes: The rooms table carries no timer/deadline column at all; the only deadline a room ever shows is read through tournament_context() from trounds.ends_at, and RoundClock counts down locally with setInterval.

units.claim: trounds.ends_at is a single absolute timestamp written when the organizer starts the timer.
units.notes: POST /{code}/timer action=start writes started_at=now, ends_at=now+minutes*60, paused_at=NULL. Minutes fall back to settings roundMinutes.

units.claim: Clients use the server's `now` only to correct a device whose clock is wrong.
units.notes: Both snapshots emit `now`; RoundClock derives offset = t.now*1000 - Date.now(), and secondsLeft() takes an offsetMs argument supplied by Play.tsx/Organize.tsx.

units.claim: Pause records paused_at.
units.notes: pausedAt is surfaced on the tournament snapshot and in the room's tournament block (table.py:284); both clients freeze the countdown at endsAt - pausedAt.

units.claim: Resume adds the paused gap back onto ends_at.
units.notes: UPDATE trounds SET ends_at = ends_at + (now - paused_at), paused_at = NULL. No-ops safely when not paused.

units.claim: A pod's extension_seconds is added on read (rather than mutating the round deadline).
remaining: GET /api/tournament/{code} returns round.endsAt unmodified and exposes pods[].extensionSeconds as a separate number
neither Play.tsx nor Organize.tsx adds myPod/pod extensionSeconds to the countdown, so the tournament-page clock for an extended table is short by the extension
units.notes: The add-on-read is implemented in exactly one place — table.py tournament_context() for the room view. The tournament snapshot never applies it.

units.claim: A judge extending one table moves only that table.
units.notes: extend with podId increments pods.extension_seconds for that pod only; without podId it moves trounds.ends_at for the whole round. Judge-resolved calls take the same per-pod path. Test asserts a 600s difference between two pods' room-side endsAt.

units.claim: Room state carries a `tournament` block with round, deadline, pause and turns.
units.notes: One query per snapshot, None for an ordinary room; block carries round, roundStatus, endsAt (extension applied), pausedAt, turnsRemaining, now, podId, table, tournament code/name.

units.claim: Tournament writes that change a clock push to the affected rooms over the room's existing WebSocket, so a pause is visible to players.
units.notes: POST /timer (start/pause/resume/extend) pushes to every room in the round; rounds/time pushes to the round; pod turn counts push to that room; resolve_call pushes only when an extension was actually granted (granted==0 changes no clock, so the omission is consistent). Non-clock writes close_round and end_tournament do not push, so a room's cached roundStatus can go stale — outside this section's claim but worth noting.

units.claim: tournaments.status runs setup → running (first round opens) → ended.
units.notes: Default 'setup'; open_round unconditionally sets 'running'; POST /{code}/end sets 'ended' and refuses while a round is active; open_round 409s on an ended tournament.

units.claim: trounds.status runs active → closed.
units.notes: Rounds are INSERTed directly as 'active' and closed to 'closed'. The schema's DEFAULT 'pending' (and its comment) is never reachable — no code path ever writes or reads 'pending'.

units.claim: pods.status runs active → awaiting_result → complete.
units.notes: Two divergences. (a) A fourth live status, 'extra_turns', is written by rounds/time when extraTurns > 0 — §2 omits it, though §5 (line 255) and §9 (line 429) do document it, and the frontend PodStatus union also omits it. (b) 'awaiting_result' is written in exactly one place, the organizer_decides time-called policy; the ordinary path (result reported or auto-recorded) goes active → complete directly, so the middle state is not a normal stage. The schema's DEFAULT 'pending' is likewise unreachable — pods are inserted as 'active'.

units.claim: Only one round is active at a time.
units.notes: Every round lookup selects the single status='active' row; close_round is the only way to clear it, and reroll reuses the active round's id rather than creating a second.

units.claim: Opening a second round while one is active is a 409 unless `reroll` is set.
units.notes: 409 'close the current round first'. With reroll the existing round's pods are deleted, the seed bumped, and the same round number re-paired.

units.claim: The documented loop create → add entrants → open round → results → close round → next round is the shape the API exposes.
units.notes: open_round pairs+seats+creates a room per pod, results write via _write_result and mark pods complete, close_round refuses while any pod is not complete or any official call is open, and the next open_round increments the round number from MAX(number).

units.claim: All §3 endpoints live under the base path /api/tournament.
units.notes: router included with prefix="/api/tournament"; every path in §3 maps to a decorated handler in tournaments.py.

units.claim: POST /api/tournament creates a tournament and requires an organizer account session.
units.notes: require_account raises 401 when no session, matching §1/§4.

units.claim: The organizer account must have an email; without one create returns 409, not 403.
units.notes: Enforced only at create time, as §6 says.

units.claim: `name` is 1–80 characters.
units.notes: Pydantic constraint, so a violation surfaces as FastAPI's 422 rather than the 400 §4 implies for malformed input.

units.claim: Unknown settings keys are dropped, not rejected.
units.notes: Whitelist is defaults_for(game); the exact expression §6a quotes is present verbatim.

units.claim: Create responds `{ "code": "K7M2Q" }`.
units.notes: Body is {"code": …, "game": …}; the client already types the extra field.

units.claim: Codes are 5 characters from an alphabet excluding I/L/O/0/1.
units.notes: "ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789" — I, L, O, 0 and 1 are all absent; 5 draws.

units.claim: GET /mine returns the calling account's tournaments, most recently active first, account session required and scoped to the caller.
units.notes: WHERE organizer_account_id = ?, ORDER BY COALESCE(last_active, created_at) DESC. Registered before /{code} so it isn't read as a code (test at :1453).

units.claim: §3 describes /mine only as 'tournaments owned by the calling account'.
units.notes: Each row also carries entrants/rounds/openCalls counts and the list is LIMIT 100 — undocumented in the contract.

units.claim: GET /{code}/plan is advisory: it recommends rounds and, where the profile defines a bracket, a cut, and nothing acts on it.
units.notes: open_round calls pair_round/seat_pods only; it never reads structure_for or cutTo, so the plan really is inert (consistent with the §10 known gap).

units.claim: §3 documents plan as taking nothing but the code and returning a recommendation.
units.notes: Handler takes no credential at all (any holder of a code sees it), accepts a `players` hypothetical-attendance query param, and raises an undocumented 409 when the game has no structures.

units.claim: GET /{code} is one snapshot, personalized in memory from one query set — no N+1, no per-viewer queries.
units.notes: Fixed query count (tournament, rounds, pods, seats, standings' 3, calls); personalization at :309-318 is pure in-memory filtering.

units.claim: Optional ?token= identifies an entrant; the organizer is recognized by cookie.
units.notes: current_account is wrapped in try/except so an anonymous read never 401s; token is scoped to the tournament code.

units.claim: The snapshot body is exactly the documented block (tournament/round/pods/myPod/me/standings/calls/isOrganizer with the listed fields).
units.notes: Every documented key exists, but the wire also carries tournament.game, pods[].turnsRemaining, standings[].wins/draws/losses, and a fully-specified calls[] element shape that §3 elides.

units.claim: pods[] carries roomCode (documented without qualification); myPod adds roomToken and mySeat.
units.notes: roomCode is null for everyone except the organizer and the viewer's own pod — a deliberate, tested rule the contract's pods[] shape does not state.

units.claim: myPod is the same shape plus roomToken and mySeat, and the room token never appears in pods[].
units.notes: roomToken is only merged into my_pod, from the viewer's own seat row.

units.claim: `me` is null when the caller is anonymous.
units.notes: Exposes public_id and name only — never wizards_email or account_id.

units.claim: `calls` is organizer only; [] for everyone else.
units.notes: calls initialized to [] and only populated under `if organizer`.

units.claim: round.now is the server clock so clients derive an offset rather than trusting the device.
units.notes: Client computes offset = now*1000 - Date.now() once per poll, exactly as documented.

units.claim: standings is always present, sorted by points, then opponents' points, then name, with 1-based dense ranks.
units.notes: sort key (-points, -opponentPoints, name.lower()); rank = enumerate index, i.e. gapless 1..N positions (ties do not share a rank).

units.claim: GET /{code}/roster is public and unauthenticated.
units.notes: Handler takes only `code` — no Request, no token.

units.claim: Roster returns name, status and entrants[{entrantId, name, claimed, dropped}] and exposes nothing else.
units.notes: Explicit column list; wizards_email and account_id are never selected. Ordering is by name COLLATE NOCASE (unspecified in §3).

units.claim: POST /{code}/claim takes no authentication — the tournament code is the only gate.
units.notes: Handler signature has no Request at all, so a session cannot leak into it; entrants.account_id is never written.

units.claim: entrantId is an opaque tournament-scoped string; the integer PK never leaves the server, an internal id posted where a public one belongs is a 404, and a public id from another tournament does not resolve.
units.notes: resolve_entrant keys on (tournament_code, public_id); every boundary in the snapshot translates. The one exception is POST /end — see 3.end-response.
units.revisionReason: Three of the four sub-claims hold and are well evidenced: entrantId on the claim path is an opaque token_urlsafe(8) string (tournaments.py:78-81, :558), resolve_entrant matches only public_id so an internal id 404s (:84-92, :594-596), and public_id is unique per row with the lookup scoped by tournament_code, so a foreign tournament's id does not resolve. But the load-bearing sub-claim — 'the integer primary key never leaves the server' — is false. POST /{code}/end returns standings_rows() untranslated (tournaments.py:658), and standings_rows emits "entrantId": e["id"], the integer PK, alongside a separate "publicId" (:225-227). Only the snapshot boundary translates (:364-368). The client even types that response as StandingRow with entrantId: string (frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:62-63, :218-219), so it silently receives integers where it expects opaque strings. The unit should be partial, not complete.

units.claim: The documented exchange is `{ "entrantId": 41 } → { "entrantToken": "…", "entrantId": 41, "name": "Ada" }`.
units.notes: ClaimBody.entrantId is typed `str` and matched against public_id, so the integer example can never succeed — it is either a 422 (type) or a 404 (no such public id). The prose four lines below contradicts its own example.

units.claim: First claim wins; a second returns 409, and the organizer can release the seat.
units.notes: Gate is `entrants.token IS NOT NULL`, cleared by release.

units.claim: collectWizardsEmail: off discards any address, optional stores it, required fails the claim with 422.
units.notes: off → wiz=None and COALESCE leaves the column untouched; required → HTTPException(422). Default is off (tournaments.py:47).

units.claim: The Wizards address is never returned by any endpoint, including the roster.
units.notes: Every response builder enumerates its columns; wizards_email appears only in the UPDATE at :614.

units.claim: POST /{code}/entrants (organizer) accepts a manual `names` list with blanks skipped and an `entrants` import list, mixable in one call, returning added[] and matched[].
units.notes: require_organizer at :531; `if not name: continue` skips blanks; both lists are concatenated into one pass.

units.claim: externalRef is unique per tournament, re-import matches on it and returns the entrant under matched, and an upstream rename updates the existing row; names are never matched on.
units.notes: Partial unique index on (tournament_code, external_ref); ref-less duplicates are inserted unconditionally at :558-564.

units.claim: POST /entrants/{id}/release (organizer) clears the token so the seat can be claimed again; idempotent.
units.notes: Unconditional `token = NULL`; repeating it is a no-op. 404 for an unknown public id.

units.claim: drop sets dropped_at and excludes the entrant from future pairings while keeping points and history; undrop clears it; both organizer-only and idempotent.
units.notes: Pairing field query filters `dropped_at IS NULL`; standings_rows still counts their seats. Minor asymmetry: undrop calls touch(), drop does not.

units.claim: POST /{code}/end is 409 while a round is open, and after ending, opening a round is 409.
units.notes: Both branches tested.

units.claim: End returns `{ "ok": true, "standings": [ … ] }` — the same standings the rest of the API speaks.
units.notes: Returns standings_rows() raw — entrantId is the integer primary key and each row also carries publicId. Every other endpoint translates at the boundary; TestEntrantIdsAreOpaque covers the snapshot and roster but not /end.

units.claim: POST /{code}/rounds pairs, seats and creates one room per pod, returning { round, pods }.
units.notes: `pods` is the integer pod count (the frontend types it as unknown[] at api.ts:205, a client-side type error, not a server one).

units.claim: reroll:false with a round already active → 409.
reroll:true discards the current round's pods and re-pairs with an incremented seed, without stopping you mid-play.
units.notes: DELETE FROM pods cascades pod_seats/pod_results (FK ON DELETE CASCADE with foreign_keys=ON); the round number is reused, seed+1. No guard on play having started, as documented. The rooms created for the discarded pods are orphaned rather than deleted.

units.claim: No undropped entrants → 400.
units.notes: The 400 exists, but the trounds row is INSERTed and committed at :730-733 before the field is checked, so the failed call leaves an empty active round behind. Untested — no test references 'nobody to pair'.

units.claim: Pairing is deterministic given (field, points, met, seed), and everything is persisted before the round is announced.
units.notes: Only randomness is random.Random(seed) / Random(seed+7919); pods, seats and rooms are all written inside the handler before it returns.

units.claim: Pod sizes never fall below 3 — remainders of 1–2 are absorbed into neighbours.
units.notes: Remainder absorption is real (pod_sizes(7,4)=[4,3], (9,4)=[5,4], (10,4)=[5,5]), but pod_sizes(2,4)=[2], (1,4)=[1] and pod_sizes(6,2)=[2,2,2] — verified by running the module. The docstring says byes are 'the caller's problem'; open_round issues none, it just seats a pod of 1–2.

units.claim: POST /rounds/time decides every pod without a result by settings.timeCalledPolicy and returns { ok, decided, policy }.
units.notes: Response is { ok, decided, extraTurns, turns, policy }; with MTG's extra_turns_at_time=5 every pod with a room goes to extra_turns and `decided` is always 0, so the documented example response cannot occur on a normal event. The handler also silently sets trounds.ends_at = now.

units.claim: Four policies: draw_all (default), draw_survivors, highest_life with genuine ties, organizer_decides moving pods to awaiting_result.
units.notes: highest_life copies the previous place on an equal life total (:952-954); organizer_decides sets status awaiting_result and returns None (:917-919). draw_all is first in the profile's tuple, hence the default.

units.claim: Eliminated players never outrank survivors, ordered by death order.
units.notes: tail is sorted by -eliminated_at and always appended after the survivors' places.

units.claim: Pods already reported are untouched and an organizer ruling is never overwritten by calling time.
units.notes: Only pods with status != 'complete' are selected, and any recorded result sets status='complete'.

units.claim: rounds/time puts each pod into extra_turns with a countdown and the policy applies at zero; a pod with no room to count in is decided immediately.
units.notes: `if extra > 0 and pod['room_code']` splits the two paths exactly as described.

units.claim: POST /pods/{pod_id}/turn takes { delta } and returns { ok, turnsRemaining, decided }.
units.notes: Reachable end to end — the player-facing control lives in the room UI, not the tournament UI.

units.claim: Any player at the table may count a turn with their entrant token, and the organizer may count for a table.
units.notes: Seated check first, organizer session as fallback; a stranger or a player at another table gets 403.

units.claim: The count may exceed where it started (MTR 2.6 slow-play turns).
units.notes: Clamped to [0, 99]; the 99 ceiling is undocumented but benign.

units.claim: §3 documents no error cases for the turn endpoint.
units.notes: 409 'time has not been called on this pod' and 409 'this pod already has a result' are both real, tested, and absent from the contract.

units.claim: POST /rounds/close refuses with 409 if any pod lacks a result or any official call is open, and both messages name the count.
units.notes: Messages are f-strings carrying the counts. An additional undocumented 409 'no round is open' guards the no-round case (:776).

units.claim: POST /pods/{pod_id}/result (organizer) takes kind/places/note/expectedVersion and returns { ok, version }.
units.notes: places carry public ids and are translated to internal ids at :850-855 (400 for an unknown entrant).

units.claim: Results are versioned, never mutated — an override appends.
units.notes: MAX(version)+1 INSERT; the test asserts both rows survive with their notes.

units.claim: A mismatched expectedVersion is a 409 with the 'someone else recorded a result' message; omitting it forces.
units.notes: Message matches the doc verbatim.

units.claim: Points come from settings.scoring (win_draw_loss or placement) and are written onto pod_seats at decision time.
units.notes: points_for is evaluated during the UPDATE of pod_seats, so later settings changes cannot rewrite history.

units.claim: kind is one of placement | draw | unfinished.
units.notes: kind is an unvalidated free string passed straight to the INSERT, and _write_result sets pods.status='complete' for every kind — so reporting 'unfinished' marks the pod finished and lets rounds/close pass. 'bye' (which points_for and the schema know about) is also acceptable but undocumented in §3.

units.claim: When a game ends in a pod's room the room reports placement from elimination order, last standing first, written with source 'auto'.
units.notes: table.report_tournament_result builds alive + eliminated-in-reverse and calls record_room_result, which writes source='auto'. §10 flags this as test-covered but not event-proven, which is consistent.

units.claim: An auto result never overwrites an organizer one; the reverse is allowed.
units.notes: Latest version's source is checked and 'organizer' short-circuits; report_result has no equivalent guard, which is the documented asymmetry.

units.claim: §3 describes the auto path as reporting the pod's game.
units.notes: record_room_result resolves the pod by room_code with no check on pod status or round status, and a room can be reopened for another game — so a second game played in a pod's room after the round closed appends a new auto result and rewrites that pod's points and the standings.

units.claim: POST /{code}/timer (organizer) supports start | pause | resume | extend.
units.notes: Also pushes the change to the pods' rooms (:1093), which §2 requires.

units.claim: start without minutes uses settings.roundMinutes.
units.notes: roundMinutes comes from the game profile's default_round_minutes.

units.claim: resume adds the paused duration to endsAt so a pause never eats clock.
units.notes: ends_at = ends_at + (now - paused_at), paused_at cleared. Resuming an unpaused round is a silent no-op (undocumented, harmless).

units.claim: extend with podId adds to that pod's extensionSeconds; without podId it extends the whole round.
units.notes: pod_in scopes the pod to this tournament (405-guard tested at test_tournaments.py:1359). The per-pod extension is applied on read in the room's tournament block. Undocumented: minutes defaults to 5 when omitted (:1081).

units.claim: No active round → 409; unknown action → 400.
One open call per pod: a second returns the existing callId with alreadyOpen: true.
units.notes: alreadyOpen is present only on the dedup branch, matching the doc's annotation.

units.claim: Tournaments with calls disabled return 409.
units.notes: allowOfficialCalls checked before the pod lookup, so a disabled event 409s even for a bogus pod id.

units.claim: The token is required and must belong to someone seated at that table; a non-seated caller gets 403.
units.notes: The old anonymous path is gone: `entrant` must be non-None and seated. Note the residual `entrant['id'] if entrant else None` at :1119 is now dead.

units.claim: POST /calls/{id}/ack (organizer) only affects open calls and returns {ok: true} even when nothing matched.
units.notes: UPDATE ... AND status = 'open'; the handler always returns ok.

units.claim: Resolve measures hand-up-to-ruling and returns openSeconds, suggestedMinutes, grantedMinutes and grantedBy (measured | judge | off).
units.notes: open_for is now - created_at; extendMinutes (including 0) overrides as 'judge'; autoExtendOnCall:false yields 'off' with 0.

units.claim: Under a minute grants nothing (MTR 2.6 sets the bar at more than one minute).
units.notes: `<= 60 → 0`, otherwise ceiling division.

units.claim: resolve closes the call and stores note as the resolution.
units.notes: status='resolved', resolved_at, resolution = body.note.

units.claim: ack and resolve are both idempotent and both return {"ok": true} even when nothing matched — a judge double-tapping should not see an error.
units.notes: ack is idempotent. resolve is not: it fetches the call without filtering on status, so resolving an already-resolved call runs the whole grant path again and adds a *second* extension to the pod — measured from the original created_at, so the second grant is larger than the first. No test covers a double resolve.

units.claim: The status codes §3 promises per endpoint (409 state conflicts, 400 malformed/nothing to pair, 403 wrong organizer, 404 no such tournament/pod, 422 required Wizards email).
units.notes: get_tournament → 404, pod_in → 404 scoped through the tournament, require_organizer → 401/403 with an AUTHZ_DENY audit event.

units.claim: Every error response is the envelope {"detail": "message"} — a single human-readable string.
units.notes: Every hand-raised HTTPException in the tournament layer passes a string, and the rate limiter's 429 body is also {"detail": str}. But no RequestValidationError/exception_handler is registered anywhere in app/ (grep for `exception_handler|RequestValidationError` returns nothing), so FastAPI's default schema-validation failure applies: 422 with `detail` as a LIST of error objects. That path is reachable on tournament endpoints — CreateBody.name is required with min_length=1 (tournaments.py:378) and TimerBody.action is required (tournaments.py:407) — so POST /api/tournament {} and POST /{code}/timer {} both return a non-string detail. frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:34 types it as `d.detail?: string` and hands it straight to TourneyError as the message, so the array surfaces to the UI unformatted.
remaining: a validation-error handler that flattens FastAPI's detail list into one string (or a spec note that 422 bodies differ)

units.claim: 400 means malformed input, or nothing to pair.
units.notes: "nothing to pair" is exact: open_round raises 400 "nobody to pair" (tournaments.py:743). Semantic malformed input is 400 as promised: unknown game (466), unknown mode (469), unrejected time-called policy (475), unknown entrant id in a result (854), unknown timer action (1091). What diverges is schema-level malformed input, which is 422 rather than 400 (no validation handler), plus one explicit 422 raised by hand in /claim (608-610). The repo's own tests encode the ambiguity: test_accounts.py:79 asserts `status_code in (400, 422)`.
remaining: §4's table has no 422 row at all, even though §3 (line 169) and the claim endpoint both promise 422

units.claim: 401 means no session where one is required.
units.notes: require_account raises 401 "sign in first" when there is no session cookie; every organizer route reaches it through require_organizer (tournaments.py:146) and create_tournament calls it directly (455). test_tournaments.py:59 asserts POST /api/tournament with no session is 401.

units.claim: 403 means authenticated, but not this tournament's organizer.

units.claim: 409 covers a result superseded by someone else's write.

units.claim: 409 covers outstanding official calls blocking an action.

units.claim: 409 covers an organizer with no recovery email attempting to host.

units.claim: 409 messages are recoverable by re-reading state and are written to be shown to a human verbatim.

units.claim: The listed statuses (400/401/403/404/409) are the meanings the tournament API carries.

(a) 422 is a real, deliberately-raised tournament status (claim with collectWizardsEmail=required, tournaments.py:609, documented in §3 line 169) plus every pydantic validation failure — it has no row in §4. (b) 409 carries several further meanings not in the enumeration: no event structures for this game (497), tournament ended (709), no round open (776/976/1064), pods with no result yet (787), time not called on this pod (1030), pod already has a result (1032), official calls disabled (1104). 429 is out of scope here since §5 documents it.

Refusals are strikes (limits.py:145-153), so overrun escalates to a ban rather than merely a 429.

units.claim: Repeat offenders escalate 1h -> 6h -> 24h -> 7d.
evidence: backend/app/limits.py:110-129 (_strike picks BAN_STEPS[min(prior, len-1)] from the persisted strike count, so the 4th and later bans stay at 7d)
backend/app/limits.py:145-149 (over-limit requests call _strike, so ordinary rate violations feed the ladder)

units.claim: Tournament clients poll at 5 s foreground, 30 s when hidden.
~50 attendees polling is ~10 req/s and sits two orders of magnitude inside the limit.
evidence: backend/app/limits.py:23 (limit is 900/60 = 15 req/s, and it is per client id, not global)
backend/app/limits.py:49-51 + :54-60 (client id is a hash of the IP, so every device behind one venue NAT is one client)
backend/app/limits.py:143-149 (the (cid, 'normal') bucket is shared across all normal traffic from that id)
units.notes: Per device the claim is right (12 req/min against 900/min). The aggregate figure the spec quotes — 50 attendees, ~10 req/s — is NOT two orders inside anything: on shared venue wifi those 600 req/min land in one client's 900/min bucket, i.e. ~67% consumed by polling alone before any writes, and overrun becomes strikes then a ban for the whole room.

SET settings exists in tournaments.py, admin.py or elsewhere. The full route list (grep of @router decorators, lines 423/446/452/484/515/529/569/589/621/633/647/661/701/769/839/965/1008/1056/1100/1125/1151) contains no settings-mutating endpoint. Reads go through settings_of() which re-merges defaults under the stored blob.

The contract's own result schema (§3, docs/tournament-api-contract.md:280) lists kind as placement | draw | unfinished — "bye" is not an accepted wire value there, though ResultBody.kind is an unvalidated str so a hand-crafted organizer POST would reach the branch. No backend test and no frontend code mentions a bye. Configured, whitelisted, and effectively dead.

units.claim: Their single `winner_id` maps to our `pod_results.places[]` — typed, ordered, and multi-place.
remaining: `pod_results` has no `places` column or child table; the ordering is written onto `pod_seats.place`/`points` (db.py:151-152, tournaments.py:829-834), so `pod_results.places[]` names a resource that does not exist in that shape.

The result `kind` is never returned by any read endpoint — the pod view in the state snapshot exposes only seats/place/points (tournaments.py:291-307) and `kind` is read internally only for standings (tournaments.py:187-191). A client or import adapter can write a type it can never read back.

units.claim: We add `entrants.external_ref` in the form `"source:id"`, which makes imports re-runnable.
units.notes: Reachable end to end: POST /{code}/entrants accepts `entrants: [{name, externalRef}]` (tournaments.py:384-387, 530-537), looks the ref up scoped to the tournament (tournaments.py:546-551), returns the existing entrant under `matched` instead of cloning (tournaments.py:554-557), and follows an upstream rename (tournaments.py:552-553). Uniqueness is enforced per tournament by a partial unique index (db.py:279-282), so the same ref can be reused across events. Covered by tests (test_tournaments.py:569-620). Two caveats that do not break the claim: the `"source:id"` shape is never validated (any string is stored, tournaments.py:541), and `external_ref` is not returned by any read endpoint (roster: tournaments.py:567-585), so a re-run must POST to discover the mapping. The frontend client only ever sends `names` (frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:192-196), which is consistent with "no adapter ships yet".

units.claim: An adapter maps `winner_id: "Draw"` to `kind: "draw"`, so no client has to special-case a magic string in an id field.
remaining: `ResultBody.kind` is a plain `str` with no enum or validator (tournaments.py:400) and `_write_result` inserts it verbatim (tournaments.py:815-816). An adapter that forwarded TopDeck's literal `"Draw"` would be accepted with a 200 and scored as a placement, not a draw (points_for compares `kind == "draw"`, tournaments.py:797), silently producing wrong points and wrong standings.
units.notes: The typed target exists and works: kind `draw` awards drawPoints to every seat (tournaments.py:797-798), backfills place 1 for all seats when the caller sends no ordering (tournaments.py:823-827), is separated from a win in standings (tournaments.py:209-213), and is produced automatically on a time-called pod with multiple survivors (tournaments.py:920-927). What is missing is the validation that would make the type actually typed at the boundary.

units.claim: An adapter maps a `table: "Byes"` row to `kind: "bye"`.
remaining: Nothing in the system can create a bye pod for the adapter to attach `kind: "bye"` to. `pod_sizes` explicitly declines to issue byes ("Byes are the caller's problem", pairing.py:44-51) and the caller, open_round, never issues one — it just seats whatever pods the pairer returned (tournaments.py:753-762). Combined with §10's "no manual pod assignment", a bye row has no home.

§3's own documentation of the result endpoint lists the accepted kinds as `placement | draw | unfinished`, omitting `bye` (docs/tournament-api-contract.md:279, mirrored in the code comment at tournaments.py:400).
units.notes: Scoring for the kind is genuinely implemented and reachable: `kind == "bye"` pays winPoints or drawPoints per the `byeScoring` setting (tournaments.py:799-800, default at tournaments.py:44), and a bye posted with no places gets every seat filled at place 1 (tournaments.py:823-827). Because ResultBody.kind is unvalidated, POSTing `kind: "bye"` on an existing pod works today.

remaining: There is no cut flag anywhere on the round model: trounds has only id/tournament_code/number/status/seed/started_at/ends_at/paused_at (db.py:127-137) and no migration adds one (db.py:224-247). An adapter has nowhere to put the second half of the mapping.
`cut_to` exists only as advisory data on a game profile's bracket (games.py:72, 92-110) surfaced by GET /{code}/plan; it never touches a round row.
units.notes: The integer half is complete (see 9.rounds-to-trounds-integer-number). §10 already declares "No top cut / playoff re-podding ... nothing performs one — there is no single-elimination path and open_round always pairs Swiss" (docs/tournament-api-contract.md:559-562), so the absent cut flag is an acknowledged gap rather than a surprise; §9's mapping table nonetheless describes a target field that does not exist.

Names are joined in at read time (tournaments.py:279-281), so an upstream rename applied during import (tournaments.py:552-553) rewrites history's display without touching any recorded result. The wire's `entrantId` is resolved to the internal id at the boundary (tournaments.py:848-855), never a name.

units.claim: An adapter expands their single `winner` per pod into `places[]`, because one winner cannot express placement, survival points, or a time-called draw.
units.notes: All three named capabilities exist. Placement: pod_seats.place plus a `placementPoints` table indexed by place (tournaments.py:801-804). Ordered multi-place from elimination order, last standing first (tournaments.py:861-883). Time-called outcomes: survivors ranked on life with shared places for ties (tournaments.py:940-957) or a survivors' draw (tournaments.py:958-962, 920-927). Points are frozen onto pod_seats at decision time (tournaments.py:833).

divergences.specSays: The entrant token in the URL "must never be logged: the reverse proxy strips query strings from access logs."
divergences.codeDoes: No log stripping exists. deploy/caddy/sites/mtg.caddy has no `log` directive and no URI rewriting, and the container runs bare `uvicorn app.main:app`, whose access log is enabled by default and records the full request target including `?token=…`. Nothing in app/main.py redacts it.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. Dockerfile's final CMD is bare `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000` with no --no-access-log, and uvicorn's access logger emits the full request target (path + query string) by default. deploy/caddy/sites/mtg.caddy contains only `encode gzip`, `header -Server`, `reverse_proxy mtg:8000` — no `log` directive, no URI rewriting, and the file's own comment says it is deliberately thin. Nothing in backend/app/main.py redacts. The spec's assertion at :36-38 that 'the reverse proxy strips query strings from access logs' is backed by nothing in this repo, and the entrant token is a bearer credential (tournaments.py:163-169).

divergences.specSays: The organizer session is carried in a cookie named `session`.
divergences.codeDoes: The cookie is named `table_session` (SESSION_COOKIE), set and read under that name everywhere.
divergences.verifierNote: Factually correct: backend/app/accounts.py:26 SESSION_COOKIE = "table_session", used by _set_cookie (:99-100), current_account (:140) and delete_cookie (:266, :344). The spec's §1 table says `session` cookie. Downgraded from medium: the cookie is httpOnly and browser-managed, so no client implementing this contract depends on the name — it is a doc inaccuracy, not a behavioural one.

divergences.specSays: A pod's extension_seconds is added on read, so a judge extending one table moves only that table.
divergences.codeDoes: Only the room snapshot adds it (table.py:273-275). GET /api/tournament/{code} returns round.endsAt with no extension applied and reports pods[].extensionSeconds separately; the tournament-page clock (secondsLeft) ignores it, so an extended table's clock on the tournament page reads short by the extension.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. Only table.py:272-275 adds extension_seconds on read (into the room snapshot's endsAt). tournaments.py:348 emits round.endsAt raw and :300 reports pods[].extensionSeconds as a separate number, and frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:301-305 secondsLeft() computes from round.endsAt alone — consumed by Play.tsx:132 and Organize.tsx:62. So the tournament page's clock for an extended table reads short by exactly the extension. The spec sentence at :55-56 is true of the room API only.

divergences.specSays: trounds.status: active → closed; pods.status starts at active.
divergences.codeDoes: Both tables declare DEFAULT 'pending' with a 'pending' state in the schema comment, but no code ever writes or reads 'pending' — rounds and pods are always inserted explicitly as 'active'. The state is defined and unreachable.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. db.py:131 and :144 both declare `status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'` with 'pending' in the schema comment, but every insert supplies a status explicitly — tournaments.py:731 inserts trounds with 'active' and :754 inserts pods with 'active'. No query anywhere reads or writes 'pending' (grep over backend/app). A defined-but-unreachable state; frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:102 even types round.status as including 'pending'.

divergences.specSays: POST /{code}/end returns { ok: true, standings: [ … ] }, and 'the integer primary key never leaves the server' — every entrantId on the wire is the opaque public id.
divergences.codeDoes: end_tournament returns standings_rows() untranslated, so each row's entrantId is the entrants table's integer primary key and each row additionally carries publicId. The snapshot endpoint translates (tournaments.py:364-368); /end is the one boundary that does not.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds, and is the sharpest finding here. tournaments.py:658 returns standings_rows(t['code']) directly, and standings_rows builds each row with "entrantId": e["id"] (the integer PK, :226) plus a separate "publicId" (:227). The snapshot endpoint strips publicId and substitutes it for entrantId at :364-368; /end is the only boundary that does not. This contradicts §3 :150-152 ('The integer primary key never leaves the server'). The client compounds it: frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:62-63 types StandingRow.entrantId as string and :218-219 applies that type to the /end response.

divergences.specSays: 'Both idempotent and both return {"ok": true} even when nothing matched — a judge double-tapping should not see an error.'
divergences.codeDoes: resolve_call selects the call regardless of status, so a second POST re-runs the extension grant: it recomputes openSeconds from the original created_at and adds another extension_seconds block to the pod. Double-tapping resolve on a 250 s call grants 5 minutes, then 5+ minutes again.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:1155-1158 selects the call by (id, tournament_code) with no status filter, so an already-resolved call is found again. :1170 recomputes open_for from call['created_at'] (which keeps growing), :1171 re-derives the suggestion, and :1183-1187 does `extension_seconds = extension_seconds + ?` again. A second organizer tap on a 250 s call grants another 5+ minutes, contradicting §3 :355-357 ('Both idempotent … a judge double-tapping should not see an error'). ack (:1128-1132) is genuinely idempotent because its UPDATE is guarded by `AND status = 'open'`; resolve has no such guard.

divergences.specSays: 'Pod sizes never fall below 3 — remainders of 1–2 are absorbed into neighbours.'
divergences.codeDoes: pod_sizes returns [n] for n < 3 (verified: pod_sizes(2,4)==[2], pod_sizes(1,4)==[1]) and honours a preferred size below 3 (pod_sizes(6,2)==[2,2,2]). open_round seats whatever comes back and never issues a bye, so a 2-entrant event gets a pod of 2 and podSize:2 produces duels throughout.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. pairing.py:48-51: `if n <= 0: return []` then `if n < 3: return [n]` — a 1- or 2-entrant field yields a single undersized pod. And the divmod path (:55-57) honours any preferred size, so podSize:2 gives [2,2,2] for six players. podSize is whitelisted (tournaments.py:60, :473) and unvalidated. tournaments.py:750-762 seats whatever pod_sizes returns and never issues a bye — the docstring at pairing.py:45-46 says byes are 'the caller's problem' and the caller does not handle them. §3 :227's 'Pod sizes never fall below 3' is true only of the remainder-absorption path.

divergences.specSays: 'Every pod without a result is decided by settings.timeCalledPolicy' with response { ok: true, decided: 3, policy: "draw_all" }.
divergences.codeDoes: Returns { ok, decided, extraTurns, turns, policy }. With the MTG profile (extra_turns_at_time = 5) every pod that has a room is moved to extra_turns instead, so `decided` is 0 on a normal event and the documented example response is unreachable. The handler also writes trounds.ends_at = now, which §3 does not mention.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds on all three points. tournaments.py:1000-1001 returns {ok, decided, extraTurns, turns, policy}, not the documented three keys. games.py:230 sets extra_turns_at_time=5 for MTG, so the branch at :988-992 moves every roomed pod to 'extra_turns' and `decided` stays 0 — the §3 :233 example response {decided: 3, policy: 'draw_all'} is unreachable on a normal MTG event. :997 additionally overwrites trounds.ends_at with now, which §3 does not mention (the client's callTime type at api.ts:210-213 also expects only {ok, decided, policy}).

divergences.specSays: 'No undropped entrants → 400.'
divergences.codeDoes: The trounds row is INSERTed and committed (db.q commits every non-SELECT) before the field is queried, so the 400 leaves an empty round in status 'active'. The organizer must then close or reroll that phantom round before a real one can open. No test exercises this path.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:730-734 INSERTs the trounds row with status 'active', and db.py:290-297 commits every non-SELECT statement, so the row is durable before the field is read at :738-741 and the 400 is raised at :743. The organizer is left with an empty active round: a subsequent POST /rounds without reroll then 409s ('close the current round first', :715). Recoverable via rounds/close, but undocumented and untested.

divergences.specSays: 'kind': 'placement' // placement | draw | unfinished
divergences.codeDoes: kind is an unvalidated string written straight into pod_results, and _write_result unconditionally sets pods.status='complete' — so a result reported as 'unfinished' counts as a finished pod and satisfies rounds/close. 'bye' is also accepted (points_for and the schema handle it) but is undocumented in §3.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. ResultBody.kind is a plain `str` defaulting to 'placement' (tournaments.py:400) with no validator, and _write_result inserts it verbatim (:815-816) then unconditionally sets pods.status='complete' (:835) — so a pod reported as kind 'unfinished' satisfies the rounds/close check at :783-787. 'bye' is likewise accepted and scored (points_for :799-800; db.py:160 lists it in the schema comment) but is absent from §3 :280's enumeration.

divergences.specSays: The pods[] element shape lists roomCode unconditionally; only roomToken is called out as seat-scoped.
divergences.codeDoes: roomCode is None for every viewer except the organizer, and re-added only onto myPod. This is deliberate and pinned by TestRoomCodesAreNotPublished, but §3's documented shape does not say so.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:296-299 sets "roomCode": p['room_code'] if organizer else None, and :313-315 re-adds the real code onto myPod only. §3 :116-118 lists roomCode in the pods[] element shape with no qualifier, and §1 :41-44 singles out only roomToken as seat-scoped. The behaviour is deliberate and pinned by TestRoomCodesAreNotPublished (tests/test_tournaments.py:1396), which is precisely why the documented shape should say so.

divergences.specSays: The GET /{code} body is the documented block: tournament{code,name,mode,status,settings,roundCount}, pods[]{podId,table,status,roomCode,extensionSeconds,seats[]}, standings[]{entrantId,name,points,opponentPoints,podsPlayed,claimed,dropped,rank}, calls[…].
divergences.codeDoes: Also returns tournament.game, pods[].turnsRemaining, standings[].wins/draws/losses, and calls[] with a concrete {id,podId,status,category,note,createdAt,openSeconds,suggestedMinutes} shape. All are consumed by the client (api.ts:62-112).
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:338 adds tournament.game, :301 adds pods[].turnsRemaining, and standings_rows :233-238 adds wins/draws/losses — none appear in §3 :112-124, and all three are declared and consumed by the client (frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:62-74, :53-58, :90-96). The calls[] part of the claim is weaker: §3 writes `"calls": [ … ]`, i.e. explicitly unspecified.

divergences.specSays: 'When a game ends in a pod's room, the room reports placement from elimination order.'
divergences.codeDoes: record_room_result resolves the pod purely by room_code and only checks whether the latest result was an organizer's. It does not check that the pod's round is still active, and rooms can be reopened for a new game, so a post-round game in a pod's room silently rewrites that pod's result, points and the standings.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. record_room_result (tournaments.py:865-869) resolves the pod by room_code alone — `ORDER BY p.id DESC LIMIT 1`, no join condition on trounds.status — and the only guard is that the latest result's source isn't 'organizer' (:872-877). Rooms are reopenable for a new game (table.py:1100-1114 sets status back to 'lobby' and clears elimination), so a casual game played in a pod's room after the round closes appends a new result version and rewrites pod_seats.place/points, and therefore the standings. §3 :295-300 describes only the in-round case.

divergences.specSays: 'GET /api/tournament/{code}/plan — Advisory only. Returns the structure recommended for the current field.'
divergences.codeDoes: Takes no credential of any kind (anyone with a code gets it, including the live undropped-entrant count), accepts a `players` query parameter for a hypothetical attendance, and raises an undocumented 409 'this game has no event structures'.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:484-485 takes no credential at all (only get_tournament), accepts a `players` query parameter for a hypothetical field, and :496-497 raises 409 'this game has no event structures'. None of the three appears in §3 :99-104, which describes only the advisory nature of the response.

divergences.specSays: Create responds { "code": "K7M2Q" }.
divergences.codeDoes: Responds {"code": …, "game": body.game}.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:481 returns {"code": code, "game": body.game}; §3 :91-92 documents `{ "code": "K7M2Q" }` only. Trivial but real.

divergences.specSays: POST /claim example: { "entrantId": 41 } → { "entrantToken": "…", "entrantId": 41, "name": "Ada" }.
divergences.codeDoes: ClaimBody.entrantId is typed str and is matched against entrants.public_id, so an integer body is rejected by validation and the string form of an internal id 404s. The response's entrantId is always the opaque public id — never 41. The example contradicts the prose immediately below it.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. ClaimBody.entrantId is typed `str` (tournaments.py:391) and this is pydantic v2 (fastapi==0.139.2 in backend/requirements.txt), which does not coerce int→str in lax mode, so the literal example body {"entrantId": 41} 422s. resolve_entrant (:89-92) matches only entrants.public_id, and the response's entrantId is row['public_id'] (:618). The §3 example at :148-149 contradicts its own prose four lines below at :152-157.

divergences.specSays: 'Tournaments owned by the calling account, most recently active first.'
divergences.codeDoes: Each row also carries entrants, rounds and openCalls counts, and the query is capped at LIMIT 100.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:433-441 selects three correlated counts (entrants, rounds, openCalls) and caps at LIMIT 100; §3 :95-97 mentions neither. Low impact — the client reads what it needs — but the cap in particular is undocumented behaviour for an organizer with many events.

divergences.specSays: The turn endpoint is documented with a body, a response and an authorization rule, and no error cases.
divergences.codeDoes: Returns 409 'time has not been called on this pod' when turns_remaining is NULL and 409 'this pod already has a result' for a complete pod; both are tested behaviour.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:1029-1032 raises 409 'time has not been called on this pod' when turns_remaining IS NULL and 409 'this pod already has a result' when the pod is complete. §3 :259-272 documents the body, response and authorization rule and no error cases.

divergences.specSays: 'Refuses with 409 if any pod lacks a result, or any official call is still open. Both messages name the count.'
divergences.codeDoes: Also returns a third, undocumented 409 'no round is open' when there is no active round.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:772-776 raises a third 409, 'no round is open', before either of the two documented checks. §3 :274-276 names only the two counted messages.

divergences.specSays: 'start without minutes uses settings.roundMinutes' — no default is given for extend.
divergences.codeDoes: extend without minutes silently defaults to 5 minutes.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. tournaments.py:1081 `mins = body.minutes or 5` — extend silently defaults to five minutes. §3 :307-310 gives a default only for `start` (settings.roundMinutes), and gives none for extend.

divergences.specSays: Errors are `{"detail": "message"}` — detail is a human-readable string.
divergences.codeDoes: No RequestValidationError handler is registered, so FastAPI's default 422 returns `detail` as a list of error objects. Reachable on tournament endpoints (CreateBody.name and TimerBody.action are required fields). The client reads d.detail as a string and shows it to the user.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. main.py registers two middlewares and four routers and no @app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError), so FastAPI's default 422 handler returns `detail` as a list of error dicts. Reachable on tournament routes: CreateBody.name (tournaments.py:378) and TimerBody.action (:407) are required, and ClaimBody.entrantId is typed str. The client at frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:32-36 does `.then((d: {detail?: string}) => d.detail)` and throws TourneyError(status, detail) — an array is then rendered into user-facing error text (Organize.tsx:73, Play.tsx:63, Host.tsx:81). Directly contradicts §4 :363.

divergences.specSays: 400 means malformed input.
divergences.codeDoes: Schema-level malformed input (missing/ill-typed body fields) returns 422, not 400; only semantic validation (unknown game, mode, timer action, entrant id) returns 400. The repo's own test asserts `in (400, 422)` rather than a single status.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds, downgraded from medium. Schema-level malformed input returns 422 (no validation handler in main.py), while §4 :367 assigns 400 to 'malformed input'; only semantic rejections are 400 (tournaments.py:466, :469, :475, :854, :1091). The repo's own test hedges — tests/test_accounts.py:79 asserts `in (400, 422)`. Same root cause as 4.error-envelope, so scored low to avoid double-counting.

divergences.specSays: Tournament paths classify as `normal` (900/60) except `POST /claim`, which is `sensitive` (20/600).
divergences.codeDoes: POST /{code}/entrants and POST /{code}/pods/{pod_id}/turn are also classified `sensitive` (20/600), because SENSITIVE_SUFFIXES contains "/entrants" and "/turn".
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. limits.py:203-204 puts '/entrants' and '/turn' in SENSITIVE_SUFFIXES, and classify (:217-222) returns 'sensitive' for any non-GET path ending in one — so POST /api/tournament/{code}/entrants (tournaments.py:529) and POST /api/tournament/{code}/pods/{id}/turn (:1008) run at 20 per 600 s, not 900/60. §5 :381-383 says tournament paths are normal 'except POST /claim and account endpoints'. Severity kept high because the client id is a hash of the IP (limits.py:49-51, :54-60): a venue behind one NAT shares a single 20-per-10-minute bucket for turn counting, and MTG's extra_turns_at_time is 5 per pod.

divergences.specSays: Polling at 5 s with ~50 attendees is ~10 req/s — two orders of magnitude inside the limit.
divergences.codeDoes: The limit is 900/60 (15 req/s) per client id, and the client id is a hash of the IP, so a venue behind one NAT is a single client: ~600 req/min of polling against a 900 req/min shared bucket, not two orders of headroom. Overrun produces strikes and eventually a ban for everyone on that IP.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. The normal budget is 900/60 = 15 req/s (limits.py:23), the identity is hmac(salt, ip) (:49-51) taken from the first X-Forwarded-For value (:57-59), and the client polls every 5 s foreground (frontend/src/tournament/useTournament.ts:11, :37). Fifty attendees on one venue NAT is ~600 req/min against a shared 900 req/min bucket — about 2/3 of the limit, not 'two orders of magnitude inside' it as §5 :387-388 claims. Overrun then feeds _strike (limits.py:145-153) for everyone on that address.

divergences.specSays: Account endpoints are `sensitive` (20/600).
divergences.codeDoes: Only /signup, /login, /recover, /password, /recovery-codes are. POST /api/account/logout, /email, /delete and PUT /api/account/notes/... classify as `normal`, and every GET account endpoint is unconditionally `normal`.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds, downgraded from medium. SENSITIVE_SUFFIXES (limits.py:208-213) covers only /signup, /login, /recover, /password, /recovery-codes, and classify short-circuits every GET to 'normal' (:218-219). POST /api/account/logout (accounts.py:262), /email (:276), /delete (:326) and PUT /api/account/notes/... (:414) all classify normal. §5 :382-383's blanket 'account endpoints' is inaccurate. Low because the endpoints left at 900/60 are session-gated and not the credential-stuffing surface the rule targets.

divergences.specSays: Nothing. §5 never names a status code, and the §4 error table lists only 400/401/403/404/409.
divergences.codeDoes: Refused requests get HTTP 429 with body {"detail": "too many requests — slow down"} and a Retry-After header in seconds. The tournament client does not handle it specially.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. main.py:107-112 returns JSONResponse({'detail': 'too many requests — slow down'}, 429, headers={'Retry-After': …}). Neither §5 :379-390 nor §4's status table :364-372 mentions 429 at all, and frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:26-38 gives it no special handling — a limited client just surfaces the message as an error. A client-visible status absent from the error table is a genuine contract gap.

divergences.specSays: "Repeat offenders escalate 1h → 6h → 24h → 7d."
divergences.codeDoes: A ban only fires after 5 refusals inside a 900 s window; bans are persisted to the bans table and retained 30 days to keep the ladder position; RATELIMIT_TRIP/BAN_ISSUED audit events are emitted; unknown-room-code guessing feeds the same ladder without being a rate violation; admin /lift clears the history.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds factually — STRIKES_BEFORE_BAN=5 within STRIKE_WINDOW=900 (limits.py:29-30, :117-120), bans persisted with 30-day retention to preserve ladder position (:35, :122-135, :184), RATELIMIT_TRIP/BAN_ISSUED events (:157-159), limiter.strike() fed by unknown-room joins (:100-110, table.py:169-183), and admin lift clearing history (admin.py:165-172). Downgraded to low: §5 :384-385 states the ladder's durations and says nothing that these contradict; they are undescribed detail rather than a conflict.

divergences.specSays: Two route classes exist: `normal` and `sensitive`.
divergences.codeDoes: A third class `socket` (60/60) exists and is live on the table WebSocket handshake, closing with code 1013 when exceeded. It shares the same limiter and ban ladder.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. limits.py:24 defines a third class "socket": (60, 60), and it is live — table.py:431-436 calls limiter.check(cid, 'socket') on the WebSocket handshake and closes with 1013 when refused, sharing the same _strike ladder. §5 :381-383 describes only normal and sensitive.

divergences.specSays: Nothing about disabling the limiter.
divergences.codeDoes: TABLE_RATELIMIT=off constructs no limiter at all and the middleware passes every request through unlimited; used by the Playwright harness.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. main.py:30 constructs no limiter when TABLE_RATELIMIT == 'off', and the middleware short-circuits on `limiter is None` (:97), so every request passes unlimited — including the WebSocket path (table.py:431-432 tolerates None). §5 says nothing about disabling it. Low: it is an operational switch, not wire contract.

divergences.specSays: "Playing needs neither an account nor an email, anywhere in the app."
divergences.codeDoes: With settings.collectWizardsEmail = "required", POST /{code}/claim rejects a seat claim with 422 unless the player supplies an email address, and stores it in entrants.wizards_email.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds (the no-UI claim). frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:186-190 exposes an optional wizardsEmail parameter, but the sole caller, Play.tsx:58, is `claimSeat(code, e.entrantId)` — no address, so a 'required' event 422s with no input anywhere to satisfy it. A grep for 'collect' across frontend/src returns zero hits, so there is also no UI to set collectWizardsEmail. A configured-but-unreachable path, exactly the class the audit was told to check for.

divergences.specSays: "The address is stored plainly and used only for recovery."
divergences.codeDoes: No code ever reads the address for recovery or anything else — /recover is recovery-code-only and there is no mail-sending code in the backend at all. The stored value is only ever coerced to a bool (hasEmail, and the hosting gate).
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. A grep for smtp/smtplib/sendmail/send_mail across backend/app returns nothing — there is no mail-sending code at all. /recover (accounts.py:304-323) authenticates on a hashed one-time code and never touches accounts.email; the column is only ever coerced to a bool, in _public (:206) and in the hosting gate (tournaments.py:458). So 'used only for recovery' (§6 :401) overstates it: the address is collected and stored and used for nothing.

divergences.specSays: Nothing in §6 describes how a player supplies the Wizards address in the client.
divergences.codeDoes: The only UI caller of claimSeat omits the wizardsEmail argument entirely, so a `required` event is unclaimable through the app — the 422 is a dead end with no input to satisfy it. There is also no UI anywhere for setting collectWizardsEmail (no hits for "collect" in frontend/src).
divergences.verifierNote: Holds (the no-UI claim). frontend/src/tournament/api.ts:186-190 exposes an optional wizardsEmail parameter, but the sole caller, Play.tsx:58, is `claimSeat(code, e.entrantId)` — no address, so a 'required' event 422s with no input anywhere to satisfy it. A grep for 'collect' across frontend/src returns zero hits, so there is also no UI to set collectWizardsEmail. A configured-but-unreachable path, exactly the class the audit was told to check for.

divergences.specSays: The §6a table and the defaults dict 'must agree'; the table enumerates 13 keys and claims a key that is not in this table cannot be stored at all.
divergences.codeDoes: The defaults dict contains 16 keys. winPoints, lossPoints and placementPoints are whitelisted on create and read by points_for, but are absent from the §6a table — so three accepted, load-bearing settings are undocumented while the section asserts completeness.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds, and §6a makes the completeness assertion explicitly ('this table and the defaults dict must agree, and a key appears here only once something reads it', :420-421). GENERIC_SETTINGS (tournaments.py:38-52) plus defaults_for's five profile-derived keys (:58-68) is 16 keys; the §6a table (:423-435) lists 13. The three missing — winPoints, lossPoints, placementPoints (:40, :42, :43) — are whitelisted on create (:472-473) and are load-bearing: points_for reads all three (:801-804). This is the exact failure mode the section says it exists to prevent, inverted.

divergences.specSays: §6a frames settings as whitelist-filtered, with the only named rejection being for keys outside the table.
divergences.codeDoes: Values are unvalidated except timeCalledPolicy: an unrecognised seatAssignment (or scoring, or a string podSize) is stored and silently behaves as the default at read time, which is a second silent-acceptance surface the section does not mention.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds narrowly. Create validates only the key set (tournaments.py:472-473) plus timeCalledPolicy (:474-475); an unrecognised seatAssignment, scoring, or a non-integer podSize is stored verbatim and silently falls through to default behaviour at read time (pairing.py:147-157 returns the shuffled default for anything but 'manual'/'by_standings'; points_for :801 treats anything but 'placement' as win_draw_loss). §6a :439-441 flags silent key-dropping as 'a sharp edge' but never mentions the equivalent silent value acceptance.

divergences.specSays: The design's `GET /calls` (staff: open + recent calls) folded into `GET /{code}`.
divergences.codeDoes: The snapshot's `calls` array is populated only when the viewer is the organizer and only for rows with `status != 'resolved'`, so the design's 'recent' (already-resolved) half is not folded in — it is not retrievable from any endpoint.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. The design's row (docs/tournament-api-design.md:75) is 'GET /calls — staff: open + recent calls'. tournaments.py:320-332 populates the snapshot's calls array only when organizer is true and only `WHERE status != 'resolved'`, so resolved calls are folded into nothing and are retrievable from no endpoint in the app. §7 :448 claims the folding is complete.

divergences.specSays: resource_direction and resource_goal are part of what a profile expresses — "which way it moves": MTG counts life down from 40 to 0; Lorcana counts lore up to a target.
divergences.codeDoes: Both fields are declared on GameProfile and set on MTG, but no code anywhere in backend/ or frontend/ ever reads them, and known_games() does not emit them. Only `resource` and `resource_start` reach runtime.
divergences.verifierNote: Holds. games.py:36-37 declares resource_direction and resource_goal and :217-218 sets them for MTG, but a grep across backend/ and frontend/src returns only those two definition/assignment sites — no reader anywhere. known_games() (:282-300) emits resource but not direction or goal, so they cannot even reach a client. divergences.specSays: modes empty means no live table state — organizers report results by hand, "which already works".
